I pulled the order-line data for every bottle SKU (21 products, category "bottles") and every jacket/outerwear SKU (21 products, category "outerwear") for Q1 2026 (Jan–Mar) and Q2 2026 (Apr–Jun), the last quarter and the one before it, using gross sales (qty × unit price, before returns/tax, per the approved metric basis).

What happened:
- Bottles: $29,127.99 (Q1) → $26,967.19 (Q2), down $2,160.80 (about 7.4%).
- Outerwear (jackets): $29,757.60 (Q1) → $29,452.64 (Q2), down $304.96 (about 1.0%, basically flat).
- Combined: $58,885.59 → $56,419.83, down $2,465.76 (about 4.2%).

Why: it is not a price move. I checked the list price on every one of these 42 products and each has had a single unchanged list price since 2025-01-01, no price-change assertions at all. The unit cost on two flagship items (Insulated bottle, Field jacket) did rise on 2026-04-01, but that only compresses margin, it does not touch the sales figures above.

The revenue drop tracks volume, not price:
- Bottles unit count fell from 702 to 674 units quarter over quarter (-4%), and the mix shifted toward lower-priced bottle SKUs, which is why revenue fell faster (-7.4%) than unit count.
- Outerwear units actually rose slightly, 478 to 483, but the mix shifted toward lower-priced jacket SKUs, so revenue was roughly flat despite more units moving.
- The single biggest dollar drop was one bottle SKU ("Bottles item 18", product:12bdcf7a), down about $1,063 quarter over quarter on its own; a few other bottle SKUs also fell $400-$700 each.

So: less bottles+jackets revenue last quarter is real (-$2,466, -4.2%), it is concentrated in bottles, and it is a volume/mix effect, not anything to do with a price change on your end.

ANSWER: Bottles+jackets gross sales fell $2,465.76 (about 4.2%) from Q1 2026 (Jan-Mar) to Q2 2026 (Apr-Jun), with the drop concentrated in bottles (-$2,160.80, -7.4%) while outerwear/jackets were roughly flat (-$304.96, -1.0%). List prices did not change on any of these products in that window, so the decline is a unit-volume and product-mix shift (fewer bottle units sold, and sales tilting toward lower-priced SKUs in both categories), not a pricing issue.
